title: Array Sum
description:
Given an integer array, return the sum of all its elements.

### Input
- Line 1: integer `n` — the number of elements.
- Line 2: `n` space-separated integers.

### Output
A single integer: the sum of the array.
editorial:
## Approach
Initialize an accumulator to 0 and add each element. Because you must read every element to know the sum, O(n) time is optimal, and only a single accumulator is needed, giving O(1) extra space.
optimal_explanation: A single pass accumulating a running total is optimal; every element must be read at least once.

starter_code.python:
import sys

def solve(nums):
    # TODO: return the sum of nums
    return 0

data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n = int(data[0])
nums = list(map(int, data[1:1+n]))
print(solve(nums))

hints: You only need to look at each element once.
Keep a running total as you scan left to right.
Watch out for negative numbers — they reduce the sum.
Sum all elements: `total += a[i]`.

prerequisites.name: Big-O / Complexity Analysis
prerequisites.what: Reasoning about how time and memory grow with the input size.
prerequisites.deep: Big-O bounds the dominant growth term and tells you whether an approach scales to the constraints. Read the limits: n up to 10^5 suggests O(n) or O(n log n), while 10^9 suggests O(log n) or O(1). Sanity-check the work against roughly 10^8 operations per second.
prerequisites.java: No API - this is analysis. Match your algorithm to the constraints stated in each problem before you start coding.
prerequisites.how: The single loop touches each of the n elements once, so the time is Theta(n) - you must read every value to sum it, and no approach is faster.

prerequisites.name: Array Iteration
prerequisites.what: Walking through elements one at a time while maintaining running state such as a sum, max, or counter.
prerequisites.deep: The workhorse of array problems: one for-loop that updates accumulators as it goes. Most linear-time solutions are just one well-chosen pass, so the real skill is deciding what state to carry so a single sweep suffices.
prerequisites.java: Use for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) or for (int x : nums). Prefer a primitive int[] over Integer[] to avoid autoboxing overhead.
prerequisites.how: You keep a running total and add each element as you pass over the array exactly once.

prerequisites.name: Integer Overflow (int vs long)
prerequisites.what: Guarding against results that exceed a 32-bit int's range of about 2.1x10^9.
prerequisites.deep: Sums, products, and reversed numbers can silently wrap a 32-bit int, giving a wrong answer with no error. The fix is a wide enough type or a modulo reduction, so estimate the maximum magnitude before choosing the type.
prerequisites.java: int overflows past ~2.1e9; long reaches ~9.2e18. Cast early with (long) a * b and accumulate sums into a long.
prerequisites.how: With up to 10^5 values as large as 10^9, the sum can reach ~10^14, which overflows a 32-bit int - accumulate into a long.

Return the input string reversed.

### Input
A single line containing a string `s` of visible characters (no spaces).

### Output
The reversed string.
editorial:
## Approach
Use two indices, one at each end, swapping and moving inward until they meet.
optimal_explanation: Each character is moved once; the output itself needs O(n) space.

starter_code.python:
s = input()

def solve(s):
    # TODO: return s reversed
    return s

print(solve(s))

hints: Think about the first and last characters swapping places.
Two pointers moving toward each other work well in-place.
Or build the result from the end to the start.
Swap s[i] and s[n-1-i] for i in [0, n/2).

prerequisites.name: Two Pointers
prerequisites.what: Two indices moving through a sequence (from both ends, or at different speeds) to replace a nested loop.
prerequisites.deep: By advancing pointers based on a comparison you explore O(n) states instead of O(n^2). Common shapes are opposite ends converging (sorted pair sums, palindromes, rain water) and fast/slow (cycle detection). Correctness hinges on why the pointer you move cannot skip a better answer.
prerequisites.java: Two int indices lo/hi (or i/j) in a while (lo < hi) loop; no special class needed.
prerequisites.how: Put one index at the start and one at the end, swap the characters, and step them toward the middle until they cross.

prerequisites.name: In-place Reversal
prerequisites.what: Reversing a segment by swapping symmetric elements, using O(1) extra space.
prerequisites.deep: Swapping a[i] with a[n-1-i] for i in [0, n/2) reverses a range without allocation. It is the building block for array rotation (reverse-whole-then-parts) and for string reversal.
prerequisites.java: A helper void reverse(int[] a, int i, int j) { while (i < j) { int t = a[i]; a[i++] = a[j]; a[j--] = t; } }.
prerequisites.how: Swapping symmetric positions reverses the text using no extra array - O(1) auxiliary space.

prerequisites.deep: Characters are small integers, so 'a'..'z' map to a 26-slot table via c - 'a'. Because Java strings are immutable, in-place character work needs a char[]. This underlies frequency counts, canonical keys, and in-place edits.

prerequisites.how: Java strings are immutable, so convert with toCharArray(), swap in place, then rebuild via new String(arr).

title: Greatest Common Divisor
description:
Compute the greatest common divisor of two non-negative integers.

### Input
Two space-separated integers `a b` on one line.

### Output
gcd(a, b).
editorial:
## Approach
Repeatedly replace (a, b) with (b, a mod b) until b is 0; a is then the gcd.
optimal_explanation: The Euclidean algorithm reduces the arguments logarithmically.

starter_code.python:
a, b = map(int, input().split())

def solve(a, b):
    # TODO: return gcd(a, b)
    return 0

print(solve(a, b))

hints: The Euclidean algorithm is the classic tool.
gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b).
Recurse/loop until b becomes 0.
When b == 0, the answer is a.

prerequisites.name: Number Theory Basics
prerequisites.what: Divisibility, gcd, and modular arithmetic facts used to reason about integers.
prerequisites.deep: Foundations like the Euclidean algorithm, prime factorization, and modular arithmetic underpin many math problems. Even simple tasks benefit from gcd/lcm identities and knowing how modulo distributes over addition and multiplication.
prerequisites.java: Math.floorMod for correct modulo of negatives; write a short gcd helper (Euclid); BigInteger has gcd() if needed.
prerequisites.how: The gcd is the largest integer dividing both inputs; Euclid's insight is that gcd(a, b) equals gcd(b, a mod b).

prerequisites.name: Recursion
prerequisites.what: A function that calls itself on smaller inputs, with base cases that stop the descent.
prerequisites.deep: Expresses divide-and-conquer and tree/graph walks naturally. Watch the recursion depth against stack limits, and whether subproblems overlap - if they do, add memoization to avoid exponential blow-up.
prerequisites.java: A private static helper that calls itself. The JVM stack handles ~10^4 depth; convert to an explicit ArrayDeque if you risk StackOverflowError.
prerequisites.how: That identity is naturally recursive - recurse on (b, a % b) until the second argument is 0, then a is the answer (a while-loop works too).

prerequisites.name: Modular Reduction
prerequisites.what: Using n % k to wrap indices around and drop redundant whole cycles.
prerequisites.deep: Modulo collapses equivalent states: rotating by k equals rotating by k % n, and hashing or bucketing uses remainders. In Java, beware that % can return a negative result for negative operands.

editorial:
## Approach
Pure simulation. Store each cell's state as a small integer: 0 neutral, 1 A, 2 B, 3 locked-A, 4 locked-B. description:

prerequisites.deep: if/else branches let your program react to data. The condition is a boolean expression built from comparisons (==, !=, <, >) and logic (&&, ||, !). Chain several with else if when there are more than two outcomes.
prerequisites.java: if (n % 2 == 0) { ... } else { ... }. Compare ints with ==, but compare Strings with .equals(), never ==.
prerequisites.how: Test 15 before 3 and 5.

title: Two Sum II (sorted)
description: Given a sorted array with exactly one solution, return the 1-based indices of the two numbers adding to `target`.
constraints:
2 ≤ n ≤ 10^4
Array is sorted ascending; exactly one answer.
editorial: With the array sorted, converge two pointers: if the pair sum is below target move left up, if above move right down.
optimal_explanation: Converging two pointers on a sorted array.
hints: Exploit the sorted order.
Two pointers from both ends adjust based on the sum.
Move left up if the sum is too small, right down if too big.

prerequisites.name: Two Pointers
prerequisites.what: Two indices moving through a sequence (from both ends, or at different speeds) to replace a nested loop.
prerequisites.deep: By advancing pointers based on a comparison you explore O(n) states instead of O(n^2). Common shapes are opposite ends converging (sorted pair sums, palindromes, rain water) and fast/slow (cycle detection). Correctness hinges on why the pointer you move cannot skip a better answer.
prerequisites.java: Two int indices lo/hi (or i/j) in a while (lo < hi) loop; no special class needed.
prerequisites.how: Converge from both ends of the sorted array.

prerequisites.name: Array Iteration
prerequisites.what: Walking through elements one at a time while maintaining running state such as a sum, max, or counter.
prerequisites.deep: The workhorse of array problems: one for-loop that updates accumulators as it goes. Most linear-time solutions are just one well-chosen pass, so the real skill is deciding what state to carry so a single sweep suffices.
prerequisites.java: Use for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) or for (int x : nums). Prefer a primitive int[] over Integer[] to avoid autoboxing overhead.
prerequisites.how: Adjust a pointer based on whether the sum is too big or small.

hints: Walk both arrays with two indices.
Always take the smaller current head.
Append the leftover tail.

prerequisites.name: Sorting
prerequisites.what: Ordering elements (usually O(n log n)) so structure like duplicates and order statistics becomes easy.
prerequisites.deep: Sorting is a preprocessing multiplier: it enables binary search, two-pointer sweeps, greedy choices, and grouping. The cost is O(n log n) comparisons, though counting/radix sort can beat that for bounded integer keys.
prerequisites.java: Arrays.sort(int[]) or Arrays.sort(T[], Comparator) / Collections.sort. For custom order use Comparator.comparingInt(...). Note primitive sort has no comparator overload.
prerequisites.how: This is the merge step of merge sort.

prerequisites.name: Priority Queue (Heap)
prerequisites.what: A structure that always yields the smallest or largest pending item in O(log n).
prerequisites.deep: A binary heap supports push and pop-min/max in O(log n) and peek in O(1). It powers greedy expansion (Dijkstra, Prim), top-k selection, and merging sorted streams, but it has no fast arbitrary lookup or deletion.

title: GCD of Array
description: Return the greatest common divisor of all elements in a non-empty array.
editorial: gcd(a,b,c,…) = gcd(gcd(a,b),c,…); accumulate a running gcd using the Euclidean algorithm.
optimal_explanation: Fold pairwise gcd across the array.
hints: gcd is associative: fold it across the array.
Use the Euclidean algorithm for each pair.

prerequisites.name: Number Theory Basics
prerequisites.what: Divisibility, gcd, and modular arithmetic facts used to reason about integers.
prerequisites.deep: Foundations like the Euclidean algorithm, prime factorization, and modular arithmetic underpin many math problems. Even simple tasks benefit from gcd/lcm identities and knowing how modulo distributes over addition and multiplication.
prerequisites.java: Math.floorMod for correct modulo of negatives; write a short gcd helper (Euclid); BigInteger has gcd() if needed.
prerequisites.how: gcd is associative — fold it pairwise.

prerequisites.name: Recursion
prerequisites.what: A function that calls itself on smaller inputs, with base cases that stop the descent.
prerequisites.deep: Expresses divide-and-conquer and tree/graph walks naturally. Watch the recursion depth against stack limits, and whether subproblems overlap - if they do, add memoization to avoid exponential blow-up.
prerequisites.java: A private static helper that calls itself. The JVM stack handles ~10^4 depth; convert to an explicit ArrayDeque if you risk StackOverflowError.
prerequisites.how: The Euclidean algorithm reduces each pair.

title: Fast Power

editorial: Binary exponentiation: while exp>0, if the low bit is set multiply the base into the result, then square the base and shift.
optimal_explanation: Exponentiation by squaring.
hints: Squaring halves the exponent each step.

prerequisites.name: Bit Manipulation
prerequisites.what: Operating on the individual binary bits of an integer with AND, OR, XOR, and shifts.
prerequisites.deep: Bit tricks give O(1) tools that replace loops: `x & (x-1)` clears the lowest set bit, `x & -x` isolates it, XOR cancels equal values, and shifting multiplies or divides by powers of two. They shine in set membership (bitmasks), parity, and counting.
prerequisites.java: Use &, |, ^, ~, <<, >>, and >>> (unsigned shift). Integer.bitCount(x) counts set bits; x & (x-1) drops the lowest one.

prerequisites.name: Integer Overflow (int vs long)
prerequisites.what: Guarding against results that exceed a 32-bit int's range of about 2.1x10^9.
prerequisites.deep: Sums, products, and reversed numbers can silently wrap a 32-bit int, giving a wrong answer with no error. The fix is a wide enough type or a modulo reduction, so estimate the maximum magnitude before choosing the type.

title: Unique Paths
description: A robot moves only right or down on an m×n grid from the top-left to the bottom-right. Return how many distinct paths exist.
editorial: dp[j] += dp[j-1] across m rows starting from all-ones — each cell sums the paths from above and from the left.
optimal_explanation: Grid DP with a rolling row.
hints: Paths to a cell = paths from above + paths from the left.
The first row and column each have exactly one path.
A single rolling row of size n suffices.

prerequisites.name: Dynamic Programming
prerequisites.what: Breaking a problem into overlapping subproblems and reusing their answers.
prerequisites.deep: Applies when there is optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems. Two styles exist: top-down memoized recursion and bottom-up tabulation. Defining the state and transition precisely is the whole game, and space can often be rolled down a dimension.
prerequisites.java: A memo HashMap or an int[]/int[][] table. For memoization initialize a sentinel with Arrays.fill(dp, -1).
prerequisites.how: Paths to a cell sum the paths from above and left.

prerequisites.name: 2-D Dynamic Programming
prerequisites.what: A table dp[i][j] indexed by two dimensions, filled from smaller states.
prerequisites.deep: Used when the state needs two coordinates: prefixes of two sequences, positions in a grid, or index-plus-capacity. The fill order must respect dependencies, and many 2-D DPs compress to one row because dp[i] depends only on dp[i-1].
prerequisites.java: int[][] dp = new int[m + 1][n + 1] filled row by row; compress to two int[] rows (prev/cur) to save memory.
prerequisites.how: A grid DP, reducible to one rolling row.

prerequisites.name: Sliding Window
prerequisites.what: A moving sub-range [left, right] whose bounds expand and contract to maintain an invariant.
prerequisites.deep: Turns 'longest/best sub-array meeting a condition' into an amortized O(n) scan: extend the right edge, and when the invariant breaks advance the left edge. Each index enters and leaves the window at most once, which is why it stays linear.

editorial: Track the farthest reach and the current level's end; each time i hits the end, take a jump and extend the end to farthest.

Extend a 'current end' greedily to the farthest reachable.
Bump the jump count when you cross the current end.

prerequisites.name: Greedy Choice
prerequisites.what: Taking the locally-best option at each step when that provably reaches a global optimum.
prerequisites.deep: Greedy is fast and simple but correct only when the problem has the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure; otherwise DP is the fallback. Proving correctness (often an exchange argument) matters more than the code.
prerequisites.java: Often just Arrays.sort plus a linear scan, or a PriorityQueue to always grab the current best.
prerequisites.how: Extend the reachable range level by level.

prerequisites.name: Breadth-First Search
prerequisites.what: Exploring a graph level by level with a queue; finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs.
prerequisites.deep: BFS visits nodes in order of distance from the source, so the first time it reaches a node is via a shortest unweighted path. It needs a queue and a visited marker and runs in O(V+E).

prerequisites.what: Using n % k to wrap indices around and drop redundant whole cycles.

prerequisites.deep: Build P[i] = a[0]+…+a[i-1]; then the sum of a[l..r] is P[r+1] − P[l] in O(1). Paired with a hash map of seen prefixes it counts subarrays with a target sum in one pass. The same idea extends to prefix XOR, products, and 2-D grids.
prerequisites.java: A long[] prefix of length n+1, or a running long combined with a HashMap<Long,Integer> of prefix counts.
prerequisites.how: The running total is the current passenger count.

prerequisites.name: Array Iteration
prerequisites.what: Walking through elements one at a time while maintaining running state such as a sum, max, or counter.
prerequisites.deep: The workhorse of array problems: one for-loop that updates accumulators as it goes. Most linear-time solutions are just one well-chosen pass, so the real skill is deciding what state to carry so a single sweep suffices.
prerequisites.java: Use for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) or for (int x : nums). Prefer a primitive int[] over Integer[] to avoid autoboxing overhead.
prerequisites.how: Track the maximum as you go.

With small n, a double loop is fine.

prerequisites.name: Big-O / Complexity Analysis
prerequisites.what: Reasoning about how time and memory grow with the input size.
prerequisites.deep: Big-O bounds the dominant growth term and tells you whether an approach scales to the constraints. Read the limits: n up to 10^5 suggests O(n) or O(n log n), while 10^9 suggests O(log n) or O(1). Sanity-check the work against roughly 10^8 operations per second.

title: Two Sum (any valid pair)

prerequisites.name: Complement Thinking
prerequisites.what: Instead of testing all pairs, ask what single value would complete the current one, and look it up.
prerequisites.deep: Reframes 'find two things that combine to T' as 'for each x, does T - x already exist?'. Paired with a hash structure this removes an entire nested loop, and the idea generalizes to differences, XORs, and remainders.

title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
description: Return the **maximum depth** (number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path) of a binary tree given in level order.
constraints:
Nodes are given in level order; `null` marks a missing child.

## Approach
Post-order recursion: depth(node) = 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right)); an empty node is 0.

An empty subtree has depth 0.
Recurse into left and right, take the max, add 1.

Edge weight = Manhattan distance between two points.
Prim's algorithm avoids materializing all O(n^2) edges up front.
Grow a tree, always adding the cheapest edge to a new point.

prerequisites.what: The cheapest set of edges connecting all nodes, built greedily by Kruskal (sort + union) or Prim (grow a tree).
prerequisites.deep: Kruskal sorts edges ascending and adds each that joins two different components (Union-Find), stopping at n-1 edges. prerequisites.what: A structure that always yields the smallest or largest pending item in O(log n).
prerequisites.deep: A binary heap supports push and pop-min/max in O(log n) and peek in O(1). It powers greedy expansion (Dijkstra, Prim), top-k selection, and merging sorted streams, but it has no fast arbitrary lookup or deletion.

title: Detect Cycle in a Directed Graph
description: A directed graph on `n` nodes has edges `u`→`v`. Return `true` if it contains a **cycle**.
editorial:
## Approach
Color nodes white/gray/black; during DFS, an edge to a gray (in-stack) node is a cycle.
optimal_explanation: DFS 3-coloring detects a back edge.
hints: DFS with three states: unvisited, in-progress, done.
A back-edge to an in-progress node means a cycle.
Mark done after exploring all descendants.
Kahn's topological sort can also detect it (leftover nodes).

prerequisites.name: Cycle Detection & Topological Sort
prerequisites.what: Finding cycles (or a valid ordering) in directed graphs with DFS 3-coloring or Kahn's indegree algorithm.
prerequisites.deep: In a DIRECTED graph, DFS colors nodes white/gray/black; an edge to a gray (still-on-the-stack) node is a back-edge — a cycle. Equivalently, Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes indegree-0 nodes; if some remain, a cycle exists. A graph with no cycle has a topological order (course schedule, build order, alien dictionary). In UNDIRECTED graphs, Union-Find or parent-aware DFS finds cycles.
prerequisites.java: Directed: int[] color (0/1/2) DFS. Kahn: int[] indeg, a queue of indegree-0 nodes, count popped == n means acyclic.
prerequisites.how: 3-color DFS back edge.

title: Detect Cycle in an Undirected Graph
description: An undirected graph on `n` nodes has edges (`u`, `v`). Return `true` if it contains a **cycle**.
editorial:
## Approach
Union each edge; the first edge whose endpoints already share a root proves a cycle.
optimal_explanation: Union-Find: an edge inside a set is a cycle.
hints: Union endpoints one edge at a time.
If both endpoints are already in the same set, this edge closes a cycle.
Union-Find handles it in near-linear time.
DFS tracking the parent also works.

prerequisites.name: Union-Find (DSU)
prerequisites.what: A disjoint-set structure that merges groups and answers 'same group?' in near-constant time.
prerequisites.deep: Each element points to a parent; a set is a tree with a representative root. `find` follows parents to the root and, with path compression, flattens the tree; `union` links one root under another, and union-by-size/rank keeps trees shallow. Together they give near-O(1) amortized operations — the go-to for connectivity, cycle detection in undirected graphs, and Kruskal's MST.
prerequisites.java: int[] parent, size; find flattens: while(parent[x]!=x){ parent[x]=parent[parent[x]]; x=parent[x]; } union links smaller under larger.
prerequisites.how: Edge inside a set is a cycle.

hints: You can finish iff the prerequisite graph is acyclic.
Topologically sort, or detect a cycle with DFS.
Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly remove zero-indegree nodes.
If any node remains, there's a cycle.

Equivalently, Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes indegree-0 nodes; if some remain, a cycle exists. A graph with no cycle has a topological order (course schedule, build order, alien dictionary). In UNDIRECTED graphs, Union-Find or parent-aware DFS finds cycles.

prerequisites.what: Ordering the nodes of a DAG so every edge points forward; impossible iff there is a cycle.

title: Is Graph Bipartite?
description: Given an undirected graph on `n` nodes (edges `u`, `v`), return `true` if it is **bipartite** — the nodes can be 2-colored so every edge joins different colors.
editorial:
## Approach
2-color via BFS; if a neighbour already has the same color as the current node, it isn't bipartite.
optimal_explanation: BFS/DFS 2-coloring across components.
hints: Try to 2-color the graph with BFS or DFS.
Color a node, then its neighbours the opposite color.
A conflict (same color on both ends of an edge) means not bipartite.
Handle each connected component.

prerequisites.name: Breadth-First Search
prerequisites.what: Exploring a graph level by level with a queue; finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs.
prerequisites.deep: BFS visits nodes in order of distance from the source, so the first time it reaches a node is via a shortest unweighted path. It needs a queue and a visited marker and runs in O(V+E).
prerequisites.java: ArrayDeque<Integer> as the queue (offer/poll) plus a boolean[] visited. Mark visited when enqueuing, not dequeuing, to avoid duplicates.
prerequisites.how: 2-color the components.

prerequisites.name: Graph Representation
prerequisites.what: Modeling entities as nodes and relationships as edges, usually an adjacency list.
prerequisites.deep: The representation dictates efficiency: adjacency lists are O(V+E) space and iterate neighbors quickly, while adjacency matrices are O(V^2) but give O(1) edge tests. Directed vs undirected and weighted vs unweighted change how you build and traverse it.
prerequisites.java: List<List<Integer>> adj, or List<int[]>[] adj = new List[n] storing new int[]{to, w} for weighted edges.
prerequisites.how: Undirected adjacency.

title: Longest Common Prefix
description: Return the longest common prefix shared by all the given strings (empty string if there is none).
editorial:
## Approach
Hold a candidate prefix; for each word, trim the candidate until the word starts with it.
optimal_explanation: Shrink a candidate prefix against each word.
hints: The common prefix can only shrink as you consider more words.
Start with the first word as the candidate prefix.
Trim it until it prefixes the next word.
A trie's single-child chain from the root gives the same answer.

prerequisites.name: Trie (Prefix Tree)
prerequisites.what: A tree where each edge is a character, so shared prefixes share a path — giving O(word length) insert and lookup.
prerequisites.deep: Each node has up to 26 children and an is-word flag. Words that share a prefix share the nodes along it, which is what makes tries shine at prefix queries: autocomplete, 'count words with prefix', word search with wildcards, and even maximum-XOR via a binary trie. The cost of any operation is the length of the word, independent of how many words are stored.
prerequisites.java: class Node { Node[] ch = new Node[26]; boolean end; } — index by c-'a'; insert walks/creates, search checks end, startsWith checks the path exists.
prerequisites.how: Single-child chain from the root.

title: Maximum XOR of Two Numbers
description: Return the maximum value of `nums[i] XOR nums[j]` over all pairs.
editorial:
## Approach
Build a bitwise trie; for each number, descend choosing the opposite bit when available to maximize the XOR.
optimal_explanation: Binary trie of bits; greedily pick opposite bits per number.
hints: Insert numbers' bits (high to low) into a binary trie.
For each number, greedily walk toward the opposite bit to maximize XOR.
Each step that can differ adds a 1 to that bit of the result.
The brute-force O(n^2) also works for small inputs.
